items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: they put together an ad hoc band that included Mingus, Archie, Rahsann and I forget who the drummer was

ctx.x: Well there were a bunch of people who were involved in this who were not necessarily on this same page musically. But they put together an ad hoc band that included Mingus, Archie, Rahsann and I forget who the drummer was, somebody else. And what they played was — even for somebody like me who is familiar with what was then called avante garde jazz — it was a total mess. And for anything, to try to appeal to the broad mass of listeners. It’s just — they should have played a tune. They played a song that people…

out there. So the whole thing was a total flop. And it was childish. And later on Andy, who is still very much around — so is Archie but I hardly ever see him, he isn’t playing anymore. He had trouble with his embouchure too. But Andy has been to the Institute quite a few times and we’ve become friendly. That’s all over, all that stuff. And Rahsann, who was a really — you know he was a terrific person but he was being used by these people. Well anyway that’s all over, that’s long — water under the bridge and we…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Except for a brief period, when he was associated with Charlie Mingus and made an album on Mingus’s Debut label which has never been reissued, but one track was reissued in this big Debut CD package which reviewed the label.

ctx.x: Yeah. He became a Billy Graham accolade. But that was another side. Lonnie was a pretty good piano player. He would occasionally – very rarely he might sit in on a jam session. He had been to New England Conservatory. He was a talented composer. Lonnie’s still around. He’s older than me. He’s now in his 80s. Except for a brief period, when he was associated with Charlie Mingus and made an album on Mingus’s Debut label which has never been reissued, but one track was reissued in this big Debut CD package which…

Floyd Campbell on washboard, Buster Bailey on clarinet, and James P. Johnson on piano. That was an incredible thing to see in the late 1940s, early 1950s. It was already a chunk of bygone history. All sorts of people that he would have. He seemed to know everybody. Then a few years later, after I got back out of the Army – we’ll come to that later – when I was hanging out at the Copper Rail in mid-Manhattan, one day suddenly Bob Maltz came in and said, “Has anybody seen Art Blakey?” That seemed like such a…
